title: asynchronous-spillback-rate-control-experiment-notes
content:
Purpose and scope:

This is an exploratory lab log for the async-"spillback" prototype and several rate-control heuristics. Goal is to reduce paging spikes and tail-latency regressions during sudden working-set growth while preserving reuse-rate for hot KV entries.

Background / motivation:
- Observed recurring tail latency correlated with NVMe paging bursts when tenant mix changes (short chat bursts + long-context requests).
- Prior approaches: aggressive eviction, prefetch, and conservative admission. All trade off either latency or reuse.
- Hypothesis: Allowing short-lived "borrowed memory" windows and controlling async spillback rate can smooth NVMe IO and preserve hot-item reuse.

Key definitions used in experiments:
- reuse_rate: fraction of KV lookups that hit resident cache within a batch window (measured per 1s sampling).
- spillback: async write/read operation to NVMe triggered when RAM budget exceeded; we treat it as background spill/restore.
- borrowed_memory_window: ephemeral overcommit allowance (MB) before starting synchronous throttling.
- async_spill_rate: bytes/sec allowed for background spillback.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- baseline: current production policy (no borrowed windows, immediate synchronous spillback when >mem_budget).
- B1: borrowed_window=256MB, async_spill_rate=200MB/s, aggressive prefetch disabled.
- B2: borrowed_window=512MB, async_spill_rate=400MB/s, prefetch for top-50 hot keys enabled.
- RC1: rate-control PID-style controller that adjusts async_spill_rate to keep NVMe queue depth < 16.
- RC2: windowed-leaky-bucket that caps bytes spilled per 1s and steps rate on staircases.

Testbed and workload:
- 4x A100 equiv nodes, CUDA 11, kernel build from main@2024-10-21 (kv-async-spillback branch).
- Workload: mixed chat+retrieve traces sampled from prod (August and October high-load days).
- Two tenant mixes: "burst-primed" (many short requests producing heavy concurrent KV lookups) and "long-tail-primed" (fewer long sequences with large seqlens).
- Monitoring: per-request tail P99/99.9 latency, NVMe iops, NVMe bandwidth, host memory usage, cache_hit_ratio (reuse_rate), eviction_count, page_reads/sec.

Selected results (aggregated, median across 6 runs):
Table-like summary (text):
- baseline (burst-primed): reuse_rate=0.61, eviction_count=28k/min, p99_latency=128ms, nvme_read_mbps=940MB/s, page_reads=18k/s
- B1 (burst-primed): reuse_rate=0.66, eviction_count=21k/min, p99_latency=102ms, nvme_read_mbps=540MB/s, page_reads=10.3k/s
- B2 (burst-primed): reuse_rate=0.70, eviction_count=18k/min, p99_latency=98ms, nvme_read_mbps=610MB/s, page_reads=11.1k/s
- RC1 (burst-primed): reuse_rate=0.68, eviction_count=19k/min, p99_latency=95ms, nvme_read_mbps=420MB/s, page_reads=7.8k/s
- RC2 (burst-primed): reuse_rate=0.65, eviction_count=20k/min, p99_latency=105ms, nvme_read_mbps=480MB/s, page_reads=9.2k/s

Notes on results and interpretation:
- Borrowed windows (B1/B2) consistently increased reuse_rate ~5-9% relative to baseline in burst scenarios, suggesting that allowing short overcommit preserves hot KV residency across microbursts.
- RC1 controller produced the best p99 latency while driving NVMe bandwidth down significantly. It dampens immediate spillback when IO queues spike, letting background async restore rehydrate hot entries.
- B2 with prefetch had a smaller bandwidth reduction than B1; prefetch helps reuse but can increase tail read amplification (prefetch misses when hotset shifts).
- RC2 (leaky-bucket) was more predictable but introduced step-change latencies when bucket drained; users saw occasional 200ms spikes correlated with bucket refill.

Micro-observations and profiling artifacts:
- Per-thread stall traces show host-GPU stall time reduced by ~12% on RC1 runs vs baseline.
- NVMe queue depth wobble is the best single predictor of upcoming p99 spikes (lead time ~200-400ms).
- Async spillback threads sometimes contend with background GC on the host; we bound background threads to cpu_set to avoid this in later runs.

Commands and config snippets (for reproducibility):
- start load harness: ./loadgen --trace=prod-2024-10-burst.json --concurrency=120 --seqdist=empirical
- runtime flags: --kv-borrowed-window-mb=256 --kv-async-spill-rate-mbps=200 --kv-spill-controller=pid --kv-prefetch-top-n=0
- pid params tuned: kp=0.6 ki=0.12 kd=0.02, sample_interval=250ms

Open questions / risks:
- Long-term correctness: will borrowed windows allow silent memory pressure growth under certain pathological steady-state loads? Need a failsafe that does hard sync spill if resident set exceeds an absolute cap for >10s.
- Multi-tenant fairness: borrowed memory could be exploited by a noisy tenant; need per-tenant budgets / credit accounting.
- Recovery behavior: when async restore floods NVMe reads after hotset shift, we observed short-term read amplification. Controller hysteresis tuning critical.

Follow-ups and next steps:
1) Implement per-tenant leased-memory accounting to prevent cross-tenant freeload during borrow windows (owner: Mateo).
2) Add NVMe queue depth telemetry to RL-based controller prototype and run RC1 vs RL-controller (owner: Evan).
3) Run 72-hour soak with RC1 on staging cluster with live shadow traffic to check for memory leak / drift (owner: Priya).
4) Draft internal playbook: "When to enable borrowed windows" with safe defaults for Dedicated vs Hosted (owner: Samira).

Errata and fringe notes (raw):
- saw one run where background spill threads reported EIO from NVMe; turned out to be test rig thermal throttling. Rerun after capping disk temp thresholds.
- small optimization idea: adaptive borrowed_window that decays when reuse_rate drops below 0.45 (heuristic).

Pointers to related docs and tickets:
- JIRA-INF-3421: async spillback design doc (linked)
- PR 891: initial async spillback impl
- confluence.redwood/kv-spillback-design-v2: design sketch and diagrams

Notes-to-self (brain dump):
- consider a hybrid: borrowed window + RC1 controller + short cold-evict watermark that preserves very-high-frequency keys (top 0.5%).
- measure impact on observed token-cost per request (if reuse increases, token cost down — capture this in next run).

End of log.
